title: What drug and alcohol training does DOT require for supervisors and drivers?
seoTitle: DOT drug and alcohol supervisor training
description: The 60 plus 60 minute reasonable suspicion training in 49 CFR 382.603, driver education under 382.601, and how FAA, FTA, FRA and PHMSA rules differ.
shortAnswer: Under 49 CFR 382.603, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires every person designated to supervise commercial drivers to receive at least 60 minutes of training on alcohol misuse and an additional 60 minutes on controlled substances use, so they can make reasonable suspicion testing decisions. Recurrent supervisor training is not required. Drivers must receive written educational materials under 49 CFR 382.601 and sign a certificate of receipt. Other DOT agencies set similar but not identical rules.
keyTakeaways: FMCSA requires at least 60 minutes of alcohol training and an additional 60 minutes of controlled substances training for anyone designated to supervise drivers, covering physical, behavioral, speech and performance indicators (49 CFR 382.603).

Only a supervisor or company official trained under 382.603 may make the observations that trigger a reasonable suspicion test, and the observations must be written up and signed within 24 hours or before results are released, whichever is earlier (49 CFR 382.307).
Drivers must receive educational materials covering 12 required topics, including Clearinghouse reporting, and must sign a statement certifying receipt (49 CFR 382.601).
Supervisor and driver training records must be kept while the person performs the function and for two years after they stop (49 CFR 382.401).

The Federal Transit Administration adds 60 minutes of drug training for every covered employee, and the Federal Aviation Administration requires recurrent training for supervisors who make reasonable cause drug testing decisions.
regulator: U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), through the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Federal Transit Administration (FTA), Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) and Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA)
appliesTo: Motor carriers and other employers of CDL drivers subject to 49 CFR Part 382
Supervisors, dispatchers, safety managers and company officials designated to make reasonable suspicion determinations
CDL drivers performing safety sensitive functions, new hires and transfers into driving positions
Aviation, transit, rail and pipeline employers covered by the equivalent FAA, FTA, FRA and PHMSA testing rules

sections.heading: What does 49 CFR 382.603 require of supervisor training?

blocks.text: Section 382.603 requires 120 minutes of training in total for each person designated to supervise drivers: at least 60 minutes on alcohol misuse and at least an additional 60 minutes on controlled substances use. The full text of [49 CFR 382.603](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-382.603) is short and worth quoting in part.

It states that the training "will be used by the supervisors to determine whether reasonable suspicion exists to require a driver to undergo testing" and that it "shall include the physical, behavioral, speech, and performance indicators of probable alcohol misuse and use of controlled substances." The final sentence settles the refresher question: "Recurrent training for supervisory personnel is not required."

items: **Duration:** two separate minimums, not a combined two hours that can be weighted toward one topic.
**Purpose:** equipping the supervisor to recognize indicators and decide whether a reasonable suspicion test is justified.
**Content floor:** physical, behavioral, speech and performance indicators for both alcohol and controlled substances.
**Frequency:** once, before the supervisor makes reasonable suspicion determinations. Employers may choose to refresh it.

blocks.text: The rule applies to persons "designated to supervise drivers", which in many carriers includes dispatchers, terminal managers and safety staff as well as line supervisors. Mapping who holds that designation is the first step in a [training needs analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-training-needs-analysis) for this obligation.

sections.heading: Why does supervisor training matter for reasonable suspicion testing?

blocks.text: Because only a trained supervisor's observations can lawfully trigger the test. [49 CFR 382.307(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-382.307) states that the required observations "shall be made by a supervisor or company official who is trained in accordance with § 382.603." A test ordered on the observations of an untrained person is exposed to challenge.

The same section sets the standard the training has to support. The determination must rest on "specific, contemporaneous, articulable observations concerning the appearance, behavior, speech or body odors of the driver", and for controlled substances the observations may include chronic and withdrawal effects. The supervisor who makes an alcohol reasonable suspicion determination may not also conduct the alcohol test.
Section 382.307 also sets deadlines that supervisors need to know in practice:

items: A written record of the observations, signed by the observing supervisor, within 24 hours of the observed behavior or before test results are released, whichever is earlier.
If an alcohol test is not given within two hours of the determination, a record of why; if not given within eight hours, attempts stop and the reasons are recorded.
A driver who shows behavioral, speech and performance indicators of alcohol misuse may not perform safety sensitive functions until a test shows less than 0.02 or 24 hours have passed.

blocks.title: Design implication
blocks.text: Training that only describes signs and symptoms leaves supervisors unable to meet the documentation and timing rules in 382.307. A practical module includes writing an observation record against a scenario and checking it for specific, articulable detail.

sections.heading: What education must drivers receive under 49 CFR 382.601?

blocks.text: Drivers must receive written educational materials explaining Part 382 and the employer's policies and procedures, before testing starts and on hire or transfer into a driving position. [49 CFR 382.601](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-382.601) also requires written notice to employee organization representatives that the information is available.

Paragraph (b) lists 12 required topics. They include the named contact for questions, which drivers and functions are covered, prohibited conduct, the circumstances and procedures for testing including post-accident testing, what counts as a refusal, consequences of violations and of an alcohol concentration of 0.02 or greater but less than 0.04, information on the effects of alcohol and drugs and on intervening when a problem is suspected, and the personal information that must be reported to the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse.

Each driver must sign a statement certifying receipt, and the employer must keep the signed certificate. Any employer policy that goes beyond Part 382, such as a stricter alcohol threshold, must be "clearly and obviously described as being based on independent authority". Part 382 does not set a minimum number of training minutes for drivers, unlike the transit rule described below.

sections.heading: How do FAA, FTA, FRA and PHMSA supervisor training rules differ?

blocks.text: Each DOT operating administration has its own training section, and the durations and refresher rules differ. The 49 CFR Part 40 testing procedures are shared, but supervisor and employee training is set in each agency's own regulation.

blocks.text: Employers regulated by more than one agency, such as a company with both CDL drivers and pipeline staff, should build to the strictest applicable rule for each role rather than assuming the FMCSA standard covers everyone. Note that FRA exempts a working supervisor who is a co-worker as defined in 49 CFR 219.5.

sections.heading: How can a motor carrier map Part 382 training obligations to evidence?

blocks.text: Part 382 training duties are easy to lose track of because they attach to different people at different moments: supervisors before their first determination, drivers on hire, the employer whenever materials change. The table sets out who owns each duty, when it bites and which record proves it. It complements, and does not duplicate, the hazmat function training covered in [DOT hazmat employee training](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training).

blocks.text: Under [49 CFR 382.401](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-382.401), records related to the education and training of supervisors and drivers "shall be maintained by the employer while the individual performs the functions which require the training and for two years after ceasing to perform those functions." For preparing those files, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: Should employers refresh supervisor training even though FMCSA does not require it?

blocks.text: Recurrent training is optional under Part 382, so the decision belongs to the employer's own risk assessment. As at November 2026 the text of 382.603 still states that recurrent training is not required, while the FAA rule for aviation employers requires a reasonable recurrent program.

Practical triggers for a voluntary refresh include a challenged or poorly documented reasonable suspicion test, changes to Part 382 such as the Clearinghouse reporting topics added to 382.601, and a long gap since a supervisor last made a determination. A documented rationale for the chosen interval, following [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles), is easier to defend than an undocumented habit.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the indicators, documentation rules and decision steps in 382.307 and 382.603 as discrete knowledge points with assessment items before any module is written, then maps them to each designated supervisor role. That lets an employer show not only that 120 minutes were delivered but which competencies each supervisor demonstrated, across FMCSA, FTA, FAA, FRA and PHMSA variants.

faqs.q: Can the 120 minutes of supervisor training be delivered online?
faqs.a: Part 382 sets duration and content but does not prescribe a delivery method, so online delivery is permitted if it meets the 60 minute minimums for each topic and covers the required indicators. Employers should keep evidence of time spent and content, since a completion flag alone does not show that each minimum was met.

faqs.q: Does a supervisor trained at one carrier need retraining at a new carrier?
faqs.a: Part 382 places the obligation on each employer to ensure its designated supervisors have received the training. A new employer can rely on prior training only if it obtains and keeps documentation showing that the training met 382.603, including both 60 minute components, and the employer's certification of compliance.

faqs.q: What must driver education materials say about the Clearinghouse?
faqs.a: Section 382.601(b)(12) requires the materials to explain that certain information must be reported to the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse: verified positive, adulterated or substituted drug results, alcohol confirmation results of 0.04 or higher, refusals, employer reports of actual knowledge of prohibited use, substance abuse professional reports, negative return to duty tests and completion of follow-up testing.

faqs.q: Is DOT supervisor training the same as hazmat or ELDT training?
faqs.a: No. Supervisor reasonable suspicion training under Part 382 is separate from hazmat employee training under 49 CFR 172.704 and from entry-level driver training under Part 380. A driver file usually contains evidence for all three, held to different retention periods.
